Evidence coming out of Virginia demonstrates an ongoing problem with teacher preparation program for general education teachers, special education teachers, and reading specialists in literacy, forcing school boards to effectively retrain new and old teachers at a considerable expense.

Out of the 31 undergraduate and graduate educator prep programs in Virginia audited by the National Council on Teacher Quality, which is NCTQ, in January, and six did not participate, only nine, which is 36% of the 25 programs reviewed, were found to accurately teach all five components of early literacy, which is phonemic awareness, systematic phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension.

Teacher preparation programs must guarantee teachers have the necessary expertise in reading instruction before they enter the classroom. So I'm here to give you a little short history about how many years we've requested institutes of higher learning to revamp their educator prep programs to teach pre-service teachers how to teach reading, writing, and spelling according to science-based reading research.

Decoding Dyslexia Virginia has been doing this work for years. Parents of students with dyslexia have noticed for decades that their kids weren't learning how to read, write, and spell, and we know this takes time. As a way to get the ball rolling, in 2016, legislators passed HB 842, which mandated a 40-minute teacher training module on dyslexia attached to state licensure.

We knew that the only approach to teach a student with dyslexia how to read is to teach them with evidence-based literacy instruction grounded in science-based reading research. That means code-based instruction that's explicit, systematic, and cumulative. That wasn't happening because teachers were not being taught this instruction in their educator prep programs.

So we started a module for all teachers. However, during this journey, we found that it wasn't just students with dyslexia who required this instruction. We came to understand it was more like 60 to 70 percent of all students who required this code-based, systematic, explicit, and cumulative instruction in order to learn how to read, write, and spell proficiently.

We realized that we didn't have the teachers who could teach reading because VA Virginia was steeped in balanced literacy and reading recovery and whole language. Therefore, we decided to focus on reading specialists, who were the ones who were providing early reading instruction. Special education teachers were more likely to agree with direct instruction, so we started with the population of teachers who needed the most change.

In 2017, SB 1516 passed in February, and this was so all districts with a reading specialist to designate one as a dyslexia advisor, acting as an expert for the district. The hope was that this reading specialist acting as a dyslexia advisor would help to change the whole language-balanced literacy culture in their district, and specifically help our families with children who had dyslexia.

Then we realized the dyslexia advisor bill was ineffective, because there was no accountability for school districts. Many stated they didn't have reading specialists, they had Title I teachers, so therefore they didn't have to have a dyslexia advisor. We still don't have any accountability for what exactly a dyslexia advisor does for the district.

It's up to the district how they want to implement the law, and still, students were not being provided appropriate instruction. Again, we went back to legislators and asked that they make certain that at least reading specialists know how to teach reading. In 2018, with SB 368, the General Assembly passed legislation requiring each education preparation program offered by a public institution of higher education or private institution of higher education that leads to a degree, concentration, or certificate for reading specialists shall include a program of coursework and other training and identification of and the appropriate interventions, accommodations, and teaching techniques for students with dyslexia or related disorders.

However, this law was not sufficient because to comply with the 2018 law, the Virginia Department of Education merely advised institutions of higher education of this new requirement and only requested that they self-report their preparation.

VDOE did not review content, syllabi, lectures, etc. to make sure there was compliance. A self-report of yes or no with no accompanying third-party audit of instructional materials for teacher prep is not an appropriate way to ensure compliance. We also found out that in Virginia, the Board of Education requires only new endorsement programs to include a review by content specialist.

So after an initial approval of educator prep programs, there is no continuing audit of syllabi and instructional materials by VDOE to get accreditation and no focus on literacy instruction. So again, legislation with no teeth is not effective, so still not good enough.

Teachers were still coming out of teacher prep not knowing how to teach reading, so we figured that perhaps professors should discuss among themselves how to get this done. So in 2020, SB 904 was passed to assist institutes of higher learning in determining how educator prep programs should teach evidence-based literacy instruction.

Higher Learning had meetings with State Council for Higher Education to discuss what evidence-based literacy should look like and how they should provide this instruction in their educator prep programs. That was four years ago, and nothing has changed. Finally, 2022, HB 419, legislators finally passed a law that requires each Virginia education preparation program offered by a public institution of higher education or private institution of higher education that provides training for any student seeking initial licensure by the Board of Education to include a program

of coursework and require all such students to demonstrate mastery in science-based reading research and evidence-based literacy instruction. The VDOE will audit each program at least every seven years to ensure compliance. The effective date will be 2024-2025 school year.

Here's your problem: The educator programs are audited in cohorts with a seven-year cycle. That cycle doesn't start until this year. That means that the programs that were accredited last year will have seven years before they're audited.

We have no baseline audit to make certain that these teacher programs are teaching teachers how to teach reading in accordance to the Virginia Literacy Act. Other states like Colorado have conducted literacy baseline audits of education preparation programs and found them to be woefully insufficient. finding compliance, it could take another three to four years to get in compliance. And that's a whole other generation of teachers and students. We simply don't have that time or money. I am making this proposal because 4.6 million children in the United States live in households where there is at least one loaded and unlocked firearm present in the household. Firearms are the number one cause of death among children under the age of 19 in the United States.

700 children die by gun suicide in the United States every year. 350 children in the United States every year obtain a firearm and inadvertently shoot themselves or someone else.
